Police sealed off roads near Haymarket, a busy theater area in London.

**June 29, 2007:** Officers disabled an explosive device found in an abandoned vehicle in Haymarket, central London. The device contained 200 liters of fuel, gas canisters and nails. A second vehicle filled with gas and nails was later discovered to have been parked only a few hundred yards from the first car, before traffic wardens towed it away early Friday morning for parking violations. Police said the two vehicles were clearly connected.

**July 21, 2005:** Two weeks after the fatal July 7 attacks, four men were accused of trying to launch another series of attacks on London’s transport system, targeting three Underground stations and a bus. The rucksack bombs they allegedly carried did not detonate.

**July 7, 2005:** Four suicide attackers blew themselves up on three Underground trains and one bus during the morning rush hour in London, killing 52 people and injuring about 700 others. Al Qaeda claimed responsibility in a video message.

**August 2004:** Counterterrorism police broke up a plan by Islamic militants to bomb locations including the Ministry of Sound nightclub and the Bluewater shopping center in southeast England. The plot involved explosives placed inside limousines and large vehicles. Seven men were found guilty in May 2007 and received prison sentences of up to 26 years.

**March 2001:** A car bomb exploded outside the BBC’s London headquarters, injuring one man. Police attributed the attack to the Real IRA, a republican breakaway group opposed to the IRA cease-fire.

**April 1999:** A nail bomb detonated inside the Admiral Duncan pub in London’s gay district, killing three people. It was the third attack in a series of nail bombings that also struck immigrant neighborhoods in the city and injured dozens. David Copeland, a 23-year-old who described himself as a “Nazi,” was given six life sentences.

**June 1996:** A large IRA bomb exploded at a shopping center in central Manchester, leaving more than 200 people injured.

**February 1996:** IRA terrorists set off a bomb in London’s Docklands district, killing two people and causing an estimated $170 million in damage. The bombing ended the group’s 17-month cease-fire.

**April 1993:** An IRA truck bomb destroyed part of London’s financial district, killing one person and injuring 44 others.

**March 1993:** Two boys, ages 3 and 12, were killed and dozens of people were hurt when two bombs hidden in litter bins exploded in Warrington, northern England. The IRA acknowledged planting the devices.

**April 1992:** A powerful IRA car bomb in London’s financial district killed three people and injured 91.

**February 1991:** IRA terrorists fired mortars at Prime Minister John Major’s offices on Downing Street. No injuries were reported.

**September 1989:** An IRA bomb exploded at a Royal Marine music school in Deal, southern England, killing 11 people and wounding 22.

**December 1988:** A Pan Am passenger jet blew up over Lockerbie, Scotland, killing all 259 people on board and 11 people on the ground. Libyan agent Abdel Basset al-Megrahi, convicted of the bombing in 2001, was granted permission this week to pursue a new appeal.

**October 1984:** Five people were killed when the IRA bombed a hotel in Brighton, southern England, where Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and members of her cabinet were staying during the Conservative Party’s annual conference.

**December 1983:** Six people died after an IRA bomb exploded at Harrods department store in London.

**July 1982:** Two IRA bombings targeting soldiers in London parks killed 11 people and injured 50.

**October–November 1974:** A series of IRA bombings in pubs in Birmingham and Guildford killed 28 people and wounded more than 200.

**February 1974:** The IRA bombed a coach carrying soldiers and their families in northern England, killing 12 people and injuring 14.

London has faced a number of serious terrorist threats and attacks in recent decades, involving both Islamist extremists and domestic violent extremists.

On June 29, 2007, police defused two linked car bombs in central London. The vehicles had been packed with fuel, gas cylinders, and nails, and were intended to cause mass casualties in busy areas of the capital. The discovery and safe disposal of the devices prevented what could have been a major attack.

Two years earlier, London had been targeted in a pair of Islamist extremist plots against the transport system. On July 7, 2005, four suicide bombers attacked three Underground trains and a bus during the morning rush hour. The bombings killed 52 people and injured about 700, making it one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in modern British history.

Just two weeks later, on July 21, 2005, four men allegedly attempted a second wave of attacks on London’s transport network. They carried rucksack bombs onto trains and a bus, but the devices failed to explode properly. Although no one was killed, the attempted attacks caused widespread disruption and heightened security fears across the city.

London had also been the focus of earlier disrupted plots. In August 2004, anti-terrorist police broke up an Islamic militant plan to bomb targets that reportedly included a nightclub and a shopping centre. The plot involved the use of explosives packed into large vehicles, indicating an intention to cause significant destruction and casualties.

Before the rise of these Islamist plots, London had already experienced other forms of terrorism. In 2001, the Real IRA carried out a car bombing outside the BBC’s headquarters, causing damage and injuries. In 1999, David Copeland carried out a series of nail bomb attacks targeting London’s gay and immigrant communities, including bombings in Brixton, Brick Lane, and Soho. These attacks killed and injured civilians and were intended to spread fear among minority communities.

Together, these incidents illustrate the range of terrorist threats faced by London, from vehicle bombs and suicide attacks to hate-driven nail bombings, and highlight the continuing importance of counter-terrorism policing and public vigilance.

Since the 1970s, mainland Britain has experienced a series of major bombings and attempted bomb attacks carried out by a range of organisations and individuals. These incidents have targeted pubs, shopping streets, transport systems, financial districts, military ceremonies, entertainment venues, airports, and public events. Taken together, they show how the terrorist threat in the UK has changed over time, from the long campaign by the IRA and later dissident republican groups, to far-right violence, to attacks inspired or directed by Islamist extremist networks including al Qaeda-linked militants.

In the 1970s, the most prominent threat came from the Provisional Irish Republican Army, which extended its campaign from Northern Ireland to mainland Britain. Bombings in cities such as London, Birmingham, Guildford, and elsewhere caused widespread fear and led to intense police operations. The 1974 Birmingham pub bombings, which killed 21 people, became one of the deadliest attacks of the period. The police response to IRA attacks often involved large-scale investigations, security alerts, evacuations, and later major reviews of criminal convictions after several miscarriages of justice were exposed.

During the 1980s, IRA attacks continued against military, political, and public targets. In 1982, bombs in Hyde Park and Regent’s Park killed soldiers during ceremonial events in London. In 1983, a bomb outside Harrods department store killed six people and injured many more. One of the most dramatic attacks came in 1984, when the IRA bombed the Grand Hotel in Brighton during the Conservative Party conference, targeting Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and her government. Thatcher survived, but five people were killed. These attacks led to heightened security around political events, military sites, and major public gatherings.

The 1990s saw further large-scale IRA bombings, particularly in commercial districts. In 1992, a bomb at the Baltic Exchange in the City of London killed three people and caused enormous damage. In 1993, the Bishopsgate bombing devastated part of London’s financial district, while the Warrington bombings killed two children and shocked the public. In 1996, the Docklands bombing ended an IRA ceasefire, and later that year a huge bomb in Manchester city centre injured more than 200 people and caused extensive destruction, though warnings allowed police to evacuate the area and prevent mass fatalities. Police and security services increasingly relied on intelligence, surveillance, vehicle checks, public warnings, and rapid evacuation procedures to limit casualties.

After the Good Friday Agreement, the main republican threat on the mainland shifted from the Provisional IRA to dissident groups such as the Real IRA. Although their activity was less sustained than the earlier IRA campaign, they remained capable of attacks and attempted attacks. Incidents in London and other areas in the early 2000s prompted continued counter-terrorism operations, arrests, and security alerts. Police treated these groups as a persistent threat, even as the overall focus of UK counter-terrorism began to shift.

In 1999, mainland Britain also faced a different kind of terrorist violence when neo-Nazi extremist David Copeland carried out nail bomb attacks in London. He targeted minority communities and the LGBT community in Brixton, Brick Lane, and Soho. The Soho bombing killed three people and injured dozens. The attacks exposed the danger posed by lone individuals motivated by far-right ideology. The police investigation used forensic evidence, CCTV, and public appeals, leading to Copeland’s arrest and conviction.

From the early 2000s onward, Islamist extremist terrorism became a central concern for UK authorities. The threat was shaped by global jihadist networks, including al Qaeda, and later by individuals radicalised through extremist propaganda. On 7 July 2005, four suicide bombers attacked London’s transport system, killing 52 people and injuring hundreds. Two weeks later, on 21 July, another group attempted similar attacks on the London transport network, but the devices failed to explode properly. These events led to major changes in policing, intelligence coordination, emergency planning, and public transport security.

Other attempted or planned attacks reinforced the seriousness of the threat. In 2006, police disrupted a plot to bring down transatlantic airliners using liquid explosives, leading to major changes in airport security rules. In 2007, attempted car bomb attacks in central London were discovered before they could cause casualties, and shortly afterward attackers drove a burning vehicle into the entrance of Glasgow Airport. Police, emergency services, and members of the public responded quickly, and the incident led to further security reviews at airports and crowded public places.

In 2017, the UK experienced several terrorist attacks, including bombings and attempted bombings. The Manchester Arena bombing in May 2017 killed 22 people, many of them children and young people leaving a concert. It was one of the deadliest terrorist attacks in Britain since 2005. The attack prompted a major police investigation, arrests, reviews of security at entertainment venues, and later public inquiries into intelligence and emergency-service responses. In September 2017, a device partially exploded on a District line train at Parsons Green in London, injuring passengers. Police quickly identified and arrested suspects, and the national threat level was temporarily raised.

More recently, in 2021, a bomb exploded in a taxi outside Liverpool Women’s Hospital. The passenger carrying the device died, while the driver escaped. Police treated the incident as terrorism and investigated the attacker’s background, motives, and possible preparation. The case again demonstrated the challenge posed by individuals acting with limited direct support but inspired by extremist ideas.

Across these decades, the targets, methods, and perpetrators have varied, but several themes remain constant. Terrorists have sought to create fear, attract publicity, cause mass casualties, damage economic life, or strike symbolic targets. Police and security responses have evolved from reactive investigations and public warnings to more integrated intelligence-led counter-terrorism, involving MI5, specialist police units, forensic teams, armed response officers, border security, and international cooperation.

The history of bombings and attempted bomb attacks in mainland Britain therefore reflects both continuity and change. The IRA campaign dominated the late twentieth century; dissident republican groups remained a concern after the peace process; far-right violence showed the danger of lone extremist attackers; and Islamist militant plots brought new challenges in the twenty-first century. Together, these incidents underline the persistent and evolving nature of terrorism in the UK, as well as the continuing importance of prevention, emergency preparedness, investigation, and community vigilance.

Here is a CNN-style chronology of major bombings and attempted bomb attacks in mainland Britain from the 1970s through the 2007 London car bomb attempts. It focuses on major incidents and does not include every hoax, warning, small device or disrupted plot.

---

## Chronology: Bombings and attempted bomb attacks in mainland Britain since the 1970s

### February 22, 1972 — Aldershot, Hampshire
**Casualties:** 7 killed, about 19 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Official IRA  
A car bomb explodes outside the officers’ mess at the headquarters of the Parachute Brigade in Aldershot. The attack is claimed as retaliation for Bloody Sunday in Northern Ireland, though most of those killed are civilian staff.

### March 8, 1973 — Old Bailey, London
**Casualties:** 1 dead, about 200 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A car bomb explodes outside the Central Criminal Court, the Old Bailey. A second bomb goes off near the Ministry of Agriculture in Whitehall. The attacks mark one of the IRA’s first major bombing operations in London during the Troubles.

### September 10, 1973 — London railway stations
**Casualties:** Several injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
Bombs explode at King’s Cross and Euston stations, part of a widening IRA campaign targeting transport and public sites in the capital.

### February 4, 1974 — M62 coach bombing, northern England
**Casualties:** 12 killed, dozens injured  
**Perpetrators:** Generally attributed to the IRA, though the group denied responsibility  
A bomb explodes on a coach carrying British soldiers and family members on the M62 motorway. It is one of the deadliest mainland attacks of the period.

### July 17, 1974 — Tower of London
**Casualties:** 1 killed, more than 40 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A bomb explodes at the Tower of London, killing a woman and injuring tourists and staff.

### October 5, 1974 — Guildford pub bombings, Surrey
**Casualties:** 5 killed, about 65 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
Bombs explode at two pubs popular with soldiers, the Horse and Groom and the Seven Stars. The case later becomes notorious for the wrongful convictions of the “Guildford Four.”

### November 7, 1974 — Woolwich pub bombing, London
**Casualties:** 2 killed, more than 30 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A bomb explodes at the King’s Arms pub in Woolwich, another venue used by soldiers.

### November 21, 1974 — Birmingham pub bombings
**Casualties:** 21 killed, more than 180 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA widely blamed; no one successfully convicted  
Bombs explode at the Mulberry Bush and Tavern in the Town pubs. The attacks are among the deadliest on the British mainland during the Troubles. The “Birmingham Six” are later cleared after wrongful convictions.

### October 10, 1981 — Chelsea Barracks, London
**Casualties:** 2 killed, dozens injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A nail bomb explodes near Chelsea Barracks, killing two civilians and injuring soldiers and passersby.

### July 20, 1982 — Hyde Park and Regent’s Park, London
**Casualties:** 11 killed, more than 50 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
Two bombs target British military bands and ceremonial troops. A car bomb in Hyde Park kills members of the Household Cavalry and horses; another device at Regent’s Park kills members of the Royal Green Jackets band.

### December 17, 1983 — Harrods bombing, London
**Casualties:** 6 killed, about 90 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A car bomb explodes outside the Harrods department store in Knightsbridge during the Christmas shopping season.

### October 12, 1984 — Brighton hotel bombing
**Casualties:** 5 killed, more than 30 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A bomb planted at the Grand Hotel in Brighton targets Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and senior Conservative Party figures during the party conference. Thatcher survives; several party officials and guests are killed or injured.

### August 1, 1988 — Inglis Barracks, Mill Hill, London
**Casualties:** 1 killed, several injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A bomb explodes at a British Army barracks in north London, killing a soldier.

### September 22, 1989 — Deal barracks bombing, Kent
**Casualties:** 11 killed, more than 20 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A bomb destroys part of the Royal Marines School of Music in Deal, killing 11 military musicians.

### July 20, 1990 — London Stock Exchange bombing
**Casualties:** No deaths; limited injuries reported  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A large bomb explodes inside the London Stock Exchange after warnings are issued. The building is badly damaged.

### February 7, 1991 — Downing Street mortar attack, London
**Casualties:** No deaths  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
Mortar shells are fired at 10 Downing Street while Prime Minister John Major and his Cabinet are meeting. One shell explodes in the garden; the Cabinet is not injured.

### February 18, 1991 — Victoria Station and Paddington Station, London
**Casualties:** 1 killed, dozens injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
Bombs explode at major London railway stations. A man is killed at Victoria Station.

### April 10, 1992 — Baltic Exchange bombing, City of London
**Casualties:** 3 killed, more than 90 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A massive truck bomb explodes outside the Baltic Exchange in the financial district, causing extensive damage and major economic disruption.

### October 12, 1992 — Sussex Arms bombing, Covent Garden, London
**Casualties:** 1 killed, several injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A bomb explodes in a pub in Covent Garden, killing one person.

### March 20, 1993 — Warrington bombings, Cheshire
**Casualties:** 2 killed, more than 50 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
Two bombs explode in litter bins in a shopping area. Two children, Johnathan Ball and Tim Parry, are killed, prompting public outrage and renewed calls for peace.

### April 24, 1993 — Bishopsgate bombing, City of London
**Casualties:** 1 killed, more than 40 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A huge truck bomb explodes in the financial district, killing a newspaper photographer and causing massive damage to buildings.

### February 9, 1996 — Docklands bombing, London
**Casualties:** 2 killed, more than 100 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A large truck bomb explodes near South Quay in London’s Docklands. The attack ends the IRA’s 1994 ceasefire.

### June 15, 1996 — Manchester bombing
**Casualties:** No deaths; more than 200 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Provisional IRA  
A massive truck bomb explodes in Manchester city centre after warnings allow evacuation. It is one of the largest bombs detonated in Britain since World War II and causes extensive damage.

### April 17, 1999 — Brixton nail bomb, London
**Casualties:** Dozens injured  
**Perpetrator:** David Copeland, far-right extremist  
A nail bomb explodes in Brixton, an area with a large Black community. It is the first in a series of attacks intended to inflame racial and social tensions.

### April 24, 1999 — Brick Lane nail bomb, London
**Casualties:** Several injured  
**Perpetrator:** David Copeland  
A second nail bomb explodes in Brick Lane, an area associated with London’s Bangladeshi community.

### April 30, 1999 — Admiral Duncan pub bombing, Soho, London
**Casualties:** 3 killed, about 70 injured  
**Perpetrator:** David Copeland  
A nail bomb explodes in the Admiral Duncan, a gay pub in Soho. Copeland is later convicted of murder for the bombing campaign.

### March 4, 2001 — BBC Television Centre bombing, London
**Casualties:** 1 injured  
**Perpetrators:** Real IRA  
A car bomb explodes outside the BBC’s Television Centre in west London. The attack is linked to the dissident republican Real IRA.

### August 3, 2001 — Ealing bombing, London
**Casualties:** Several injured  
**Perpetrators:** Real IRA  
A car bomb explodes in Ealing, west London, causing injuries and significant damage to shops and buildings.

### November 3, 2001 — Birmingham car bomb attempt

Four suicide bombers attacked the London transport network during the morning rush hour, detonating bombs on three Underground trains and a bus. Fifty-two victims were killed and more than 700 injured. The attacks were the deadliest terrorist incident in Britain since Lockerbie.

---

### **2005: Failed London transport attacks**
**July 21, 2005 — London**  
Two weeks after the 7/7 attacks, four men attempted to detonate bombs on three Underground trains and a bus. The devices failed to explode properly, and there were no fatalities. The attackers were later convicted.

---

### **2007: Haymarket and London car bomb attempts**
**June 29, 2007 — Central London**  
Two car bombs were discovered in London’s West End, including one outside the Tiger Tiger nightclub near Haymarket. The devices failed to detonate and were made safe by police. The attempted attacks were linked to Islamist extremists.

---

### **2007: Glasgow Airport attack**
**June 30, 2007 — Glasgow, Scotland**  
A day after the Haymarket devices were found, two men drove a burning vehicle into the entrance of Glasgow Airport. The attack caused injuries but no deaths among the public. One attacker later died from burns, and the other was convicted.

---

### **2013: Birmingham mosque bombs**
**June–July 2013 — West Midlands**  
Ukrainian student Pavlo Lapshyn planted explosive devices near mosques in the West Midlands after murdering a Muslim pensioner in Birmingham. The devices caused limited physical injuries but were intended to terrorise Muslim communities. Lapshyn was later convicted.

---

### **2017: Manchester Arena bombing**
**May 22, 2017 — Manchester**  
A suicide bomber detonated a device at the end of an Ariana Grande concert at Manchester Arena. Twenty-two people were killed and hundreds injured. The attack was one of the deadliest in Britain in decades and prompted a major public inquiry into security and emergency response failures.

---

### **2017: Parsons Green attempted bombing**
**September 15, 2017 — London**  
A device partially exploded on a District line train at Parsons Green Underground station, causing burns and panic injuries but no deaths. The attacker, Ahmed Hassan, was later convicted of attempted murder.

---

**Summary:**  
The incidents span multiple eras of terrorism in Britain: the IRA’s mainland bombing campaign from the 1970s to the 1990s, far-right violence in 1999, Islamist attacks and attempted attacks in the 2000s and 2010s, and dissident republican activity after the Good Friday Agreement. The deadliest incidents on British soil in this period were the **1988 Lockerbie bombing**, the **2005 London transport attacks**, and the **2017 Manchester Arena bombing**.
